Yeah, I know what this is. It's **Chlorine**, a Minecraft performance mod you wrote for the Fabric mod loader.

**What the mod does**

It targets CPU-side lag and laptop power use. It leaves chunk rendering to mods like Sodium. The README groups the features like this:

- **Adaptive client tuning:**
  - It watches a rolling FPS average and lowers simulation distance when FPS drops, then raises it again after a cooldown.
  - It can also scale entity distance and drop the particle setting as a last resort.
  - A fast-travel governor lowers simulation distance during Elytra or Riptide movement.
  - It deliberately leaves render distance alone, to avoid big chunk-graph rebuild hitches.
- **Server and gameplay side:**
  - It staggers AI for distant classic mobs and for Brain-driven mobs (villagers, piglins, etc.).
  - It merges nearby item entities and XP orbs.
  - It caches font widths.
  - It can log slow server ticks as a warning, without changing behavior.
- **Client effects and power saving:** it caps FPS when the window is unfocused, and it budgets sounds and particles per tick. It also throttles beacon beams and portal particles.

**How the folder is laid out**

- The repo has three version snapshots side by side: `1.0.0-26.2`, `1.0.2-26.3` and `1.0.3-26.3`. Each is a full Gradle project.

- Inside each project, `src/main` holds the shared and server code, and `src/client` holds the client-only code, as in a Fabric split-environment project. The `mixin` folders hold the injections into Minecraft.
- `disabled-mixins/` holds a `LightmapThrottleMixin` you turned off.
- `.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes a GitHub Pages site. Your latest commits touch a "release selector" that shows legacy releases, and the last commit deleted the old `chlorine-website` directory.

I found six new optimizations that Chlorine doesn't already do. I checked each one against the 26.3 code to confirm the expensive part really exists. None of them is built yet, so none has been measured.

### Best for 1% lows (stutters)

**1. Smooth out light updates when new chunks arrive.** Vanilla works through queued lighting a few jobs per frame. Once 1000 or more jobs pile up, it runs all of them in a single frame. That happens every time you fly an elytra into new terrain, teleport or join a world, and it causes the hitch you feel as a 1% low. The fix spreads that work over a small time budget each frame (about 1–2 ms). The trade-off is that new chunks may look dark for a few frames. The code is in `ClientLevel.pollLightUpdates()`.

**2. Spread out the 5-minute autosave (singleplayer).** Every 5 minutes, autosave saves every changed chunk in a single server tick. On a laptop, where the built-in server shares CPU cores with rendering, that shows up as a regular stutter. Vanilla already has a slower background save (20 chunks per tick), so autosave could leave some chunks for that and still save everything. This one is about saving your world, so it's the highest risk of the six and needs careful testing. The code is in `MinecraftServer.autoSave()` and `ChunkMap.saveAllChunks()`.

### Best for raw FPS

**3. Scale down ambient block effects when FPS is low.** Every client tick, vanilla checks 1,334 random blocks around you for torch flames, dripping water, leaf particles and similar effects. When FPS drops, we can lower that number using the same low-FPS signal the sound and particle limits already use. You'd see slightly fewer ambient particles. The code is in `ClientLevel.animateTick()`, where the 667 is a fixed number in the loop.

**4. Stop drawing sign text you can't read anyway.** Vanilla draws the text on every sign within 64 blocks, but you can't read it past about 20 blocks. Skipping text beyond a set distance helps a lot in bases with walls of labelled storage. The code is in `AbstractSignRenderer.submitSignText()`. ImmediatelyFast has an experimental sign-text option, but it caches the text rather than skipping it, so the two work together.

**5. Draw far-away dropped items as one model.** Vanilla draws a stack of items on the ground as several copies of the item model. Beyond about 16 blocks, one copy looks the same. This helps mob farms and pairs with the item merging Chlorine already does. The code is in `ItemEntityRenderer.submitMultipleFromCount()`.

**6. Shorten how far chests, banners and skulls draw when FPS is low.** These are drawn as full 3D models every frame up to 64 blocks away. When FPS is low, we could shorten that distance. EntityCulling only skips the ones hidden behind walls; this would cover the visible ones far away. The setting is `BlockEntityRenderer.getViewDistance()`.

### Ideas I checked and dropped
- **Entity shadows:** vanilla already fades shadows out by 16 blocks, so culling them saves nothing.
- **Rain and snow:** vanilla already draws these efficiently. The splash particles are already covered by Chlorine's particle limit.
- **The parked lightmap throttle:** the lighting code was rewritten in 26.x (`Lightmap` plus `LightmapRenderStateExtractor`), so there's little left to save. I'd leave it disabled.

One more thing: a lot of 1% lows on Java come from garbage-collection pauses, and that's controlled by JVM launch flags that a mod can't change. A short section on the website about JVM flags might help players more than any single mixin.

**Low-FPS switch:** Features 3 and 6 only turn on when FPS is low. A new shared switch in [RenderPressure.java](1.0.5-26.3/src/client/java/com/chlorine/client/RenderPressure.java) handles that. It turns on below 35 FPS and only turns off again above 45, so effects don't flicker when FPS hovers around 35.

**Settings screen:** The toggles are in two new categories in the Mod Menu config screen, "Frame Smoothing" and "Render LOD".

**Why the autosave change can't lose chunks:**
- Vanilla's background saver only drops a chunk from its list once that chunk is saved.
- The limit only applies inside the 5-minute autosave. Shutdown, `/save-all`, the pause-menu save and chunk unloading all save everything as normal.
- Worst case, some chunks get written a few seconds later than vanilla's autosave would have written them.

**Sodium:** It draws block entities through the same vanilla method that feature 6 hooks, so feature 6 works with Sodium installed. I checked this in the Sodium 0.9.2 jar.

### What to look for when you test
- **Fly an elytra fast into new terrain.** That should feel smoother. New chunks may look dark for a few frames, which is the expected trade-off.
- **Go to a wall of signs and back away.** The text should disappear around 24 blocks.
- **Stand near a mob farm and back off.** Item piles should turn into single items past about 16 blocks.
- **Force low FPS** (high render distance or shaders) near a storage room. Chests should stop drawing past about 32 blocks.
- **Leave a singleplayer world running past the 5-minute mark** and watch for the regular stutter. The server test couldn't cover this, since an autosave never ran with nothing changed in the world.

1. **Adaptive chunk upload budget** (biggest win). Each frame Sodium allows up to 30% of the frame time for uploading built chunks to the GPU, and never less than 10 ms. At 144 FPS a frame is only about 7 ms, so that 10 ms minimum can be longer than a whole frame while you explore. Chlorine would lower the minimum when frames are already slow, and keep it while loading into a world so chunks still fill in fast. The cost is that new terrain appears a little later while flying.
2. **Smaller "rebuild right now" radius under pressure.** Block changes within 16 blocks are rebuilt on the main thread straight away, and finished chunks within 64 blocks are shown immediately. TNT, piston farms and redstone cause bursts of this. 3. **Keep culling off the main thread during fast travel.** When the camera moves quickly, Sodium switches its visibility check onto the main thread. I found six new optimizations that Chlorine doesn't already do. I checked each one against the 26.3 code to confirm the expensive part really exists. None of them is built yet, so none has been measured.

### Best for 1% lows (stutters)

**1. Smooth out light updates when new chunks arrive.** Vanilla works through queued lighting a few jobs per frame. Once 1000 or more jobs pile up, it runs all of them in a single frame. That happens every time you fly an elytra into new terrain, teleport or join a world, and it causes the hitch you feel as a 1% low. The fix spreads that work over a small time budget each frame (about 1–2 ms). The trade-off is that new chunks may look dark for a few frames. The code is in `ClientLevel.pollLightUpdates()`.

**2. Spread out the 5-minute autosave (singleplayer).** Every 5 minutes, autosave saves every changed chunk in a single server tick. On a laptop, where the built-in server shares CPU cores with rendering, that shows up as a regular stutter. Vanilla already has a slower background save (20 chunks per tick), so autosave could leave some chunks for that and still save everything. This one is about saving your world, so it's the highest risk of the six and needs careful testing. The code is in `MinecraftServer.autoSave()` and `ChunkMap.saveAllChunks()`.

### Best for raw FPS

**3. Scale down ambient block effects when FPS is low.** Every client tick, vanilla checks 1,334 random blocks around you for torch flames, dripping water, leaf particles and similar effects. When FPS drops, we can lower that number using the same low-FPS signal the sound and particle limits already use. You'd see slightly fewer ambient particles. The code is in `ClientLevel.animateTick()`, where the 667 is a fixed number in the loop.

**4. Stop drawing sign text you can't read anyway.** Vanilla draws the text on every sign within 64 blocks, but you can't read it past about 20 blocks. Skipping text beyond a set distance helps a lot in bases with walls of labelled storage. The code is in `AbstractSignRenderer.submitSignText()`. ImmediatelyFast has an experimental sign-text option, but it caches the text rather than skipping it, so the two work together.

**5. Draw far-away dropped items as one model.** Vanilla draws a stack of items on the ground as several copies of the item model. Beyond about 16 blocks, one copy looks the same. This helps mob farms and pairs with the item merging Chlorine already does. The code is in `ItemEntityRenderer.submitMultipleFromCount()`.

**6. Shorten how far chests, banners and skulls draw when FPS is low.** These are drawn as full 3D models every frame up to 64 blocks away. When FPS is low, we could shorten that distance. EntityCulling only skips the ones hidden behind walls; this would cover the visible ones far away. The setting is `BlockEntityRenderer.getViewDistance()`.

- **Entity shadows:** vanilla already fades shadows out by 16 blocks, so culling them saves nothing.
- **Rain and snow:** vanilla already draws these efficiently. The splash particles are already covered by Chlorine's particle limit.
- **The parked lightmap throttle:** the lighting code was rewritten in 26.x (`Lightmap` plus `LightmapRenderStateExtractor`), so there's little left to save. I'd leave it disabled.

One more thing: a lot of 1% lows on Java come from garbage-collection pauses, and that's controlled by JVM launch flags that a mod can't change. A short section on the website about JVM flags might help players more than any single mixin.

I built a Memory Governor, but it can't do what you asked for. A mod can't replace Java's garbage collector or stop leaks. The collector is picked by the JVM flags in your launcher. It builds cleanly, but I haven't run it in the game or committed it.

**What it does** ([MemoryGovernor.java](src/client/java/com/chlorine/client/MemoryGovernor.java), checked every 5 seconds):
- **Cache trimming:** when the heap passes 85% (adjustable), it empties Chlorine's own collision cache.
- **GC on world leave:** after you leave a world it requests one collection on a background thread. It runs at most once a minute and won't freeze the menu. If your launcher uses `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`, the JVM ignores it.
- **Leak watch:** it tracks memory still in use right after each collection. If that grows across six collections by at least 8 MB, it logs one warning. It only logs, and the cause is often another mod.

All four settings are in a new "Memory Governor" category. I also added `CollisionCache.clear()` for the trimming.

I haven't measured any FPS or frame-time gain, and I expect little. Most Minecraft stutter from memory comes from the JVM flags, not the mod. For that, G1 or Generational ZGC with 6–8 GB allocated usually helps the most.
